claims.text: A directly deposited elemental Cr coating on fuel-cladding-grade zirconium alloy is prone to Cr–Zr interdiffusion during high-temperature steam exposure.
Cr–Zr interdiffusion causes premature failure of directly deposited Cr coatings under high-temperature steam exposure.
Adding a thin, continuous YSZ interlayer between the zirconium-alloy substrate and Cr coating will suppress high-temperature Cr–Zr interdiffusion.
Suppressing Cr–Zr interdiffusion with a YSZ interlayer will prevent premature coating failure.
The YSZ-interlayer coating system will retain the full protective performance of Cr under normal subcritical-water conditions.
A YSZ interlayer functions as a physical barrier to Cr–Zr atomic exchange during high-temperature exposure.
YSZ has inherently low ionic diffusivity.
YSZ is chemically stable against Cr.
YSZ is chemically stable against Zr.
The low diffusivity and chemical stability of YSZ slow or prevent Cr–Zr atomic interdiffusion.
Inhibiting Cr–Zr interdiffusion inhibits intermetallic formation at the coating–substrate interface.
Intermetallic formation at the Cr–Zr interface produces brittle phases that compromise coating integrity.
Avoiding brittle interfacial phases will maintain Cr-coating integrity during accident-relevant temperature excursions.
Relative to directly deposited Cr, the YSZ-plus-Cr system will exhibit significantly less Cr–Zr interdiffusion at elevated temperature.
Normal subcritical-water operation can be bounded by reactor-coolant conditions below approximately 400 °C.
YSZ interlayer thickness and deposition conditions affect the balance among diffusion-barrier effectiveness, coating adhesion, and long-term stability.

Failure to obtain a statistically significant reduction in Cr–Zr interdiffusion or improvement in coating integrity under high-temperature steam relative to the direct-Cr control would falsify the proposed barrier effect.
